title: Animals: Structure and Function
seo_title: Grade 11 Biology (SBI3U): Animals: Structure and Function Worksheets (Ontario)
standard_text: The structure and function of the digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems in animals; how they interact; and disorders and lifestyle factors that affect them. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Biology, Grade 11, University Preparation (SBI3U), Strand E: Animals: Structure and Function)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Biology (SBI3U) worksheets on animal structure and function: digestion and enzymes, the respiratory system, gas exchange, the heart and blood vessels, blood and health. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Digestion, respiration and circulation work together to supply every cell.
key_sub: Large surface areas and short distances make exchange fast.
body_html:
How to think about it

The digestive system breaks large food molecules into small ones (amylase: starch to sugars; protease: proteins to amino acids; lipase: fats to fatty acids and glycerol) that are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine.

In the lungs, oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out. The heart pumps blood in two circuits: the right side sends it to the lungs, the left side to the body. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins bring it back, and capillaries are where exchange happens.

Example

Which enzyme starts digesting starch in the mouth?

Starch is a carbohydrate.

Answer: salivary amylase

Example

Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the right?

The left side pumps to the whole body.

Answer: it must pump blood at higher pressure around the body

Common mistakes

  • Saying arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood: the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood.
  • Thinking digestion happens mainly in the stomach: most absorption is in the small intestine.
  • Mixing up breathing (moving air) and cellular respiration (releasing energy).

faq.q: Why do alveoli have thin walls?
faq.a: A short diffusion distance lets oxygen and carbon dioxide move between air and blood quickly.
They give the small intestine a huge surface area for absorbing digested food.

items.q: Food passes through the stomach. Which part does it enter next?
items.e: The order is: mouth → esophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus.

items.q: What is the product of digestion by peptidase (erepsin)?
items.e: Peptidase (erepsin) digests peptides into amino acids.

items.q: Pulmonary ventilation is 12.0 L min⁻¹ at 30 breaths per minute. Calculate the tidal volume.
items.e: Tidal volume = ventilation ÷ breathing rate = 0.400 L.

items.q: How does asthma reduce the rate of gas exchange?
c: the airways narrow, so less air reaches the alveoli
items.e: Inflamed bronchioles produce mucus.

items.q: Food enters the rectum. Which part did it come from?
items.e: The order is: mouth → esophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus.

items.q: What happens during inspiration?
c: the external intercostal muscles and diaphragm contract, so the volume of the thorax increases
items.e: Air pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system does this? It stores bile until it is needed in the small intestine.
items.e: The gall bladder: It stores bile until it is needed in the small intestine.

items.q: A person has a tidal volume of 0.45 L and breathes 24 times per minute. Calculate the pulmonary ventilation rate.
items.e: Pulmonary ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate = 10.8 L min⁻¹.

items.q: Which enzyme digests starch into maltose?
items.e: Each enzyme is specific to its substrate.

items.q: What is the product of digestion by pancreatic amylase?

items.q: Which part of the digestive system does this? It moves food from the mouth to the stomach by peristalsis.

items.q: What is the main job of the mouth?
c: It stores bile until it is needed in the small intestine.
It churns food and makes gastric juice with protease and acid to start digesting proteins.
Teeth break food into small pieces and saliva starts to digest starch.
It is the opening through which feces leave the body.
items.e: The mouth: Teeth break food into small pieces and saliva starts to digest starch.

items.q: A person breathes 12 times a minute with a tidal volume of 450 mL. How much air does he breathe in each minute?
items.e: Pulmonary ventilation = rate × TV = 12 × 450 = 5400 mL.

items.q: In a healthy adult, TV = 500 mL, IRV = 2500 mL, ERV = 1000 mL and RV = 1200 mL. What is the functional residual capacity?
items.e: Functional residual capacity = ERV + RV = 2200 mL.

items.q: What are the C-shaped rings in the trachea made of?
items.e: They keep the trachea open.

items.q: During inspiration (breathing in), what happens to the ribcage?
items.e: Breathing in: external intercostals and diaphragm contract, ribs up and out, thorax volume up, pressure down, air rushes in. Breathing out is the reverse.

items.q: During expiration (breathing out), what happens to the air pressure in the lungs?
items.e: Breathing in: external intercostals and diaphragm contract, ribs up and out, thorax volume up, pressure down, air rushes in. Breathing out is the reverse.

items.q: In a healthy adult, TV = 500 mL, IRV = 2900 mL, ERV = 1050 mL and RV = 1200 mL. What is the total lung capacity?
items.e: Total lung capacity = RV + ERV + TV + IRV = 5650 mL.

items.q: A person breathes 16 times a minute with a tidal volume of 450 mL. How much air does he breathe in each minute?
items.e: Pulmonary ventilation = rate × TV = 16 × 450 = 7200 mL.

items.q: What is emphysema?
c: a disease in which the alveolar walls are damaged, reducing the surface area
items.e: Cigarette smoking is a major cause.

items.q: Where does gas exchange take place in the lungs?
items.e: Their walls are one cell thick.

items.q: How do xerophytes reduce water loss?
c: more stomata on the upper surface
sunken stomata, rolled leaves and hairs that trap moist air
items.e: These reduce the water potential gradient.

items.q: What is tidal volume?
c: the maximum volume of the lungs
the volume of air breathed in or out in one normal breath
the volume left after breathing out
items.e: About 0.5 L at rest.

items.q: About what percentage of inspired air is carbon dioxide?

c: remove amino acids from the ends of polypeptides
hydrolyze peptide bonds in the middle of chains
items.e: Endopeptidases act within the chain.

items.q: How is air carried to the cells of an insect?
items.e: Gas exchange happens at the tracheole ends.

What do bile salts do in digestion?
items.e: This gives lipase a larger surface area.

items.q: How does the percentage of nitrogen in expired air compare with inspired air?
items.e: Nitrogen is not used by the body.

items.q: A block of agar is 3 cm × 2 cm × 5 cm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio, as x : 1.
Which enzyme digests starch to maltose?
items.e: Made in the salivary glands and pancreas.

items.q: What happens during normal expiration?
c: the ribs move up and out
the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles relax
items.e: Expiration is mostly passive.

items.q: Why can insects not grow very large?
c: gases move along the tracheae mainly by diffusion, which is slow over long distances
items.e: Muscle movement can help ventilate the tracheae.

items.q: Why do single-celled organisms not need a gas exchange system?
c: they have a large surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion is fast enough
items.e: Larger organisms need specialized surfaces.

items.q: How many heartbeats does a healthy adult have each minute at rest?
items.e: It is set by the SA node.

items.q: Cardiac output is 8.25 L min⁻¹ and stroke volume is 110 mL. Calculate the heart rate.
items.e: HR = CO ÷ SV = 8250 ÷ 110 = 75 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: One cardiac cycle on an ECG lasts 0.80 s. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
items.e: Heart rate = 60 ÷ 0.80 = 75.0 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: Which part of the blood or heart is responsible for B and T cells of the immune response?
items.e: Lymphocytes: B and T cells of the immune response.

items.e: The coronary artery carries oxygenated blood to the muscle of the heart wall.

items.e: HR = CO ÷ SV = 8800 ÷ 110 = 80 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: Does the pulmonary vein carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?

items.q: Stroke volume is 60 mL and heart rate is 150 beats per minute. Calculate cardiac output in L min⁻¹.

items.q: Which antibodies are in the plasma of blood group AB?
items.e: Blood group AB has no antibodies in the plasma.

items.q: Which blood group is the universal donor?
items.e: Its cells carry no A or B antigen.

items.q: What is the stroke volume of a healthy adult heart?
items.e: Cardiac output = 72 × 70 mL ≈ 5 L per minute.

items.q: Which part of the blood or heart is responsible for carrying the impulse down the interventricular septum?
items.e: Bundle of His: carrying the impulse down the interventricular septum.

items.q: Why does high blood pressure increase the risk of coronary heart disease?
c: Fatty deposits build up in the coronary arteries.
Nicotine and carbon monoxide damage artery walls and raise blood pressure.
items.e: In coronary heart disease, the coronary arteries are narrowed by fatty deposits (atherosclerosis), so less oxygen reaches the heart muscle.
